blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: This tree follows the topics and the problem list of NeetCode's roadmap (the NeetCode 150), with a learning page written for this site for each topic. The explanations and Java templates are ours; the problems belong to LeetCode, and each one links to its LeetCode page.

2-D DP is the same recipe as 1-D DP (state, transition, base case, order) with **two changing quantities** in the state, so the table has two dimensions: a position in two strings (`dp[i][j]`), a grid cell, or an item index and a remaining capacity.

| Family | State `dp[i][j]` | Transition idea | Problems |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Grid paths** | Ways or cost to reach cell (i, j) | From the cell above or to the left | Unique Paths |
| **Two strings** | Answer for the first i characters of A and first j of B | Characters equal: take the diagonal; else best of dropping one | Longest Common Subsequence, Edit Distance, Interleaving String, Distinct Subsequences |
| **Knapsack** | Using the first i items with capacity j | Take the item or leave it | Coin Change II, Target Sum, Partition Equal Subset Sum |
| **Intervals** | Best for the range i..j | Try every split point k | Burst Balloons |
| **Matching** | Do the first i of the text match the first j of the pattern | Cases for `.` and `*` | Regular Expression Matching |

"two strings", "subsequence", "edit", "match", "grid with obstacles", "knapsack", "target sum with each item once", "interleave". Whenever the input is two sequences and you compare prefixes, think `dp[i][j]`.
blocks.title: Signal words

blocks.text: **Drawing the table** on paper with the base row and column filled in, and shading which cells each cell depends on, is the fastest way to find the transition and the loop order. If `dp[i][j]` only reads the previous row, keep **one row** and cut memory from O(n·m) to O(m).

blocks.title: Dp2d.java

blocks.text: **What to notice.** Two loop-direction rules decide correctness. For **combinations** (Coin Change II) put the coins in the outer loop; swapping the loops counts *permutations* (1+2 and 2+1 as different). For **0/1 knapsack** with a one-row table, iterate the capacity *downwards* so an item cannot be used twice; for **unbounded** knapsack (coins reusable) iterate upwards.

- **Off-by-one between string index and table index.** Row `i` is "the first i characters", so the character is `charAt(i - 1)`.
- **Missing base row and column.** Edit Distance needs `dp[i][0] = i` and `dp[0][j] = j`, not zeros.
- **Wrong loop order** when compressing to one row (see above).
- **Memory.** A 5000 x 5000 `int` table is 100 MB. Keep two rows when only the previous row is read.
- **Recovering the actual answer** (the subsequence, the edit script) needs the full table, walked backwards from `dp[n][m]`.

`dp[i][j]` is the fewest operations to turn the first i characters of A into the first j of B. If the last characters match, nothing is needed: `dp[i-1][j-1]`. Otherwise take one plus the best of replacing the last character (`dp[i-1][j-1]`), deleting from A (`dp[i-1][j]`) or inserting into A (`dp[i][j-1]`). The base cases are converting to or from the empty string.
blocks.title: Interview angle: Explain the recurrence for edit distance.
Key points
blocks.text:
- 2-D DP is the 1-D recipe with two state variables: draw the table and mark its dependencies
- Strings: `dp[i][j]` is about the first i and first j characters; use `charAt(i - 1)`
- Fill the base row and column deliberately
- Combinations need the items in the outer loop; 0/1 knapsack loops capacity downwards
- Keep one row when only the previous row is read
- Rebuilding the actual answer needs the whole table

blocks.title: Practise and track them
blocks.text: Open **Practice** in the top bar and choose **2-D Dynamic Programming** (under DSA by topic) to tick problems off, keep notes on each one, and add problems of your own.

items.question: Why does Coin Change II put the coin loop outside and the amount loop inside?
items.answer: Processing one coin at a time allows only combinations in non-decreasing coin order, so each combination is counted once. With the amount loop outside, the same coins in different orders would be counted separately.

items.question: Why must the 0/1 knapsack's inner loop run downwards?
items.answer: `reachable[sum - n]` must still refer to the state *before* this item was considered. Running upwards would already include the item, letting it be used several times, which is the unbounded problem.

items.question: What is the time and space of Longest Common Subsequence and how can the space shrink?
items.answer: O(n·m) time and space. Because each row only reads the previous row, two rows (or one row plus a variable for the diagonal) bring the space down to O(min(n, m)); you then lose the ability to reconstruct the subsequence.
